utterances.text: Later on in your testimony we're going to talk about situations where, for example, you and your interpreters had to do things such as move through police check-points or army check-points or NLA check-points. When you were in such situations during the crisis time of 2001, would it -- were you able to observe whether the policemen, NLA members, and your interpreters appeared to understand each other?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you able to understand, in these situations, were you able to observe whether a person who was speaking either Albanian to your interpreter or Macedonian to your other interpreter, whether their conversation was being understood or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah. Most likely in the result, that means when there was a conversation between, for example, policemen and my Macedonian interpreter, then -- and we could pass in the result, then it was a successful conversation they have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Did, for example, persons manning check-points, when they were speaking to your -- to you through an interpreter, did they ever switch to other languages?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Sometimes policemen or also NLA fighters changed into German, because a lot of Macedonians worked in Germany. So they were just happy to speak some words German and to talk about the history, where they stood in Germany, where they worked in Germany, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So at that point you could personally participate in --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- the conversations? Finally, or perhaps penultimately, during your time in Macedonia in 2001, did you ever learn that one of your interpreters had seriously or significantly misinterpreted a conversation or incorrectly, significantly and incorrectly interpreted a conversation? ?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No. I never -- I never saw that they were doing significantly a mistake. What they did sometimes, especially when you was talking to a politician, that they translated one word wrong and a politician would like to say something more soft.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: More moderate.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah, more moderate than it was said. So, for example, we had one interview with the -- it was the president of Macedonia, Boris Trajkovski and when the interpreter translated in English to me, the president corrected him with one word so that it was more moderate what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you publish many articles in your newspaper in Germany regarding the events in Macedonia during 2001?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In times where the fightings erupted or where German soldiers were involved, in which case ever, I reported daily, and in times where the conflict was not on a such high level of intensity, I was not reporting -- yeah, I say weekly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. In 2001, did anyone ever question, particularly did anyone of your sources, did anyone ever contact you and complain that you had written something that was wrong or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If I could turn your mind, please, to the events in Macedonia in 2001. You mention, I believe, that you returned to Macedonia in 2000 -- excuse me, in January of that year. At some point, did you start creating perhaps what we could call a living book?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. That was part of my daily work to cover the situation in Macedonia because, especially between January and March I had to return sometimes to Germany and to be updated when I was returning to Macedonia, it was necessary for me to be aware of the current situation. So I started drawing a map, how the situation develops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. And were you in Macedonia, for example, during July and August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you continue working on this, if we can call it the living book, during those months?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have some materials that we would like to distribute to the Chamber, and to the -- we have extra copies for Defence counsel. And if one copy can be given to the witness, please, we would be very grateful. And, Your Honours, and Mr. Hutsch, if you could please turn to tab 1 in the binder. This is from 65 ter number 295. And we just need to look at one of the maps in this range which has the ERN N001-7245.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, this map that is in front of you, is this a map that you created?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, that's a map that I created in the time between the Aracinovo crisis and the beginning of August 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we just wait a moment, please, because we're going to see now electronic copies appearing in front of us. The hard copy is actually easier to see, I think. And there are a lot of red markings on this map. And can you tell us, please, what these red markings describe?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: So this red mark, it describes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You know what I might ask you to do, so that the Judges can see, can understand what you're speaking about, I may ask you to mark bits of the electronic version that's in front of you. If we can look, please, at -- if I can turn your attention perhaps to the lower left-hand part of this map. We see sort of a circle in red, and then we see some arrows going in different directions. Can you tell us what you drew there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: It's, I guess, this area that shows us that we have here the position of the 115 NLA Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: This brigade is doing reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I stop you for a moment. Next -- to the left of that big circle that you have just drawn, could you please write the numbers 115.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And did you personally observe members of the 115th Brigade in this area?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. I had contact with the commander of this brigade and I visited him. That was a commander with his fighting name Miskoja. That means the teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Up above, if we go in a vertical line up the map, we see a smaller circle. You see that smaller circle in red?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: I think this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, sure. Let's start with that one. What were you marking there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: There were south-east -- south-west of Cacanik, the Kosovo city Cacanik close. Behind the border in Kosovo there have been logistical centre of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So can you -- if you can, please, can you draw -- again with your pen, because it is difficult to see on the map, could you highlight the line of the border with Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: So that's, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And so if I understand the map that you have drawn, members of the 115th Brigade at the time were based, if I can use that term, just inside the Kosovo border but were sending reconnaissance units into Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No, that is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. This brigade, 115, have been in the -- in the town of Radusa and Radusa is -- it is close to the border.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: I would say it's divided nearly by the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But it is on the Macedonian side?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: It is on the Macedonian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Then up above a little bit higher further into what we now see is Kosovo, there is another small circle. What were you indicating there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: There have been -- that is also the area hardly west from Cacanik, parts of brigade 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: This brigade -- parts of this brigade fought in Aracinovo - Aracinovo is here - and have been withdrawn by NATO troops or by United States troops in June 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And was there some kind of a base at that point?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: They had some training camps there, in the area of the village Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "they," who is "they?"

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: "They" is the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And did you observe personally the training camps in that area?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. I observed -- or I monitored this training camp several times, and it has been there during the complete war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. To the left of that circle that you drew showing the area where the part of the 114th Brigade was at that time, could you just write the letters -- hold on, hold on, 114. Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, I see you have just -- Mr. Hutsch, I don't know what you just wrote?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Parts, parts --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: -- of Brigade 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If could you to me a favour, let me please lead you through this so there is no confusion, all right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand you have a lot of knowledge about this matter. A bit the to the east you have just drawn a red circle around a smaller circle. What were you indicating there on this map?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: As being the main logistical assembly for the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you personally observe this logistical assembly area?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And perhaps you could place the number -- so we can indicate that logistical area, perhaps you could above that circle write the letter L, capital L.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm reminded again, Mr. Hutsch, that so far, our efforts to pause between question and answer are less than perfect. So we need to try to keep that in mind. Next -- or to the right of the area that you marked as the logistical base we see a small half circle just on the Macedonian side of the border. What was that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That is the village of Tanusevci and village of Tanusevci was the spear point of the NLA when they entered Macedonia in January 2001, and they kept this village as a stronghold till the end of the war. Is it the part of an old smuggling route and it was one of the main doors for the NLA to enter Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, above -- perhaps on the Kosovo side of the border above that the area of Tanucevske, could you write a capital T, please.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And now if you could move further toward the right, we see a series of areas that have been indicated by you sort -- almost forming a vertical line. And perhaps if we could go from the top down. If could you simply describe what each point is.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: So what we have here in common on this line are the positions of Brigade 113.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say brigade, again, we're talking about a NLA brigade?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly, an NLA brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: This brigade had in this moment, all in all, five infantry battalions with this position. They were supported by a so-called artillery battalion which was located here. They had some mortar positions here and here. And they did some reconnaissance in this part. In their back, the parts of Brigade 114 were doing reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So this would be the part of the 114th Brigade that had not left Macedonia after the fighting around Aracinovo?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And just to help us understand the whole context of this, could you also draw a circle roughly about where the village of Ljuboten would be?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Ljuboten is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And perhaps just so that the record is clear, could you just write the number 1 underneath that circle.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And all of these positions, then, if I can understand, you personally observed while you were in Macedonia in July/August 2001?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And was this the situation close to the 10th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And perhaps if this exhibit could be taken off the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, I'd like to ask you to turn your mind to the events of Friday, the 10th of August, 2001. Can you recall a particular event that happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: So I was investigating a story about the peace process in Ohrid, in Skopje, while one of the interpreters got a phone call about an incident that took place in the north of Ljuboten where members of the army had been trapped into a ambush of the NLA, and unknown of couple of soldiers had been killed, in this moment unknown couple of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And can you recall which unit of the Macedonian army had suffered that ambush?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: They have been members of the 2nd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Guardist Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So after you received this information, what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: We decided to go north to Ljuboten area. There was another incident that made us clear that we should go into this area, because while we were going to -- through Skopje, a column of police vehicles drove also in north direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "a column of police vehicles," can you describe what kind of vehicles that you saw?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Normal Steyr-Puch trucks with police officers in camouflage uniforms and a BTR-80.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Any jeeps?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Some jeeps in this column as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you know these were police vehicles as opposed to vehicles of some other entity?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: They were marked by the police plate and they were -- the police officers were wearing the police badges at their uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And when you refer to the police plate, are you referring to a licence plate?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you, please, to take a look at what is tab 5 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this photograph is on page 6 of the court binder. Actually, I may be misspeaking, I apologise. I am misspeaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we turn to this, you mentioned that these reserve police officers in the truck had camouflage uniforms with a badge or insignia. What did this insignia say?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: This insignia was on a dark ground, with the letters or the capitals PM, Policija Macedonia and they were surrounded in the lower part by some leaves that -- that this circle are wearing the formal Roman Ceasars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to page 23 of the court binder. And, Witness, I'll let you know which photograph I'm speaking about. Witness, and if I could direct the parties' attentions to photograph B of the court binder. Witness, can you take a look at that photograph on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Exactly these badges they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And so those were the police badges that you saw on these gentlemen in the trucks?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but could the Prosecution perhaps put it on the screen so that we can see what document and what picture. I think it is being done, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit P35.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so -- yeah, there it is. And so when you saw this column, you decided to follow it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you notice whether the policemen in the back of the truck were armed or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: The policemen, so far as we could see, monitor, they were armed with the normal Kalashnikov rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: We went to Radishan, and in the -- in the -- in the end of the village, if you -- when you -- and you're passing from Skopje, there was a temporarily check-point from -- from police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was that check-point then at the end of the village close-- going in the direction of the village of Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to turn, please, to tab 3 of the binder. And this is 65 ter number 295. Okay. Witness, did you create this?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. That was -- I create this during my statement here in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you look over towards the left-hand side of this map, or portion of a map, first we see -- we see in small letters the village name Radishan and above that we see a circle. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you draw a larger circle around that with your red pen. It didn't work, I'm sorry, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And we can see that you wrote the letters pointing to the inner circle above Radisani, you wrote the word CP. What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That stands for check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And a bit above and to the right, a bit to the north-east, we see a couple of small circles and then another marking above it. Can you explain what those small markings are?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: These marking are first a mortar position, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. And a mortar position which what force?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: By the -- probably by the Macedonian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And then below that, we see two little circles.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: These are two target areas, where these mortars fired in while I was in the area of the check-point, and I could monitor myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And that -- what is now a sort of dark red filled-in circle, would that be filling in the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps just -- just beneath that dark red circle could you write a capital letter L.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Were you allowed to pass through the check-point where you were at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: At that time we wasn't allowed to pass the check-point. We just were allowed to stay around the check-point in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And help us, please. I'm not sure if you said this already. Who was manning this check-point?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: This check-point had around eight, up to ten, police officers. It seems to me that two of them have been active police officers, because they were wearing the normal, I will say, blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: And six, up to eight have been reserve officers, because, yeah, they were wearing the camouflaged uniform and they were drinking some beer, and this was always in an indicia for reserve officers, because when they came to their duty, they drank beer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And about how much time did you spend at this check-point or around this check-point?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Around this check-point, roughly around three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would seek it tender this map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P291, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hutsch, if you and the parties could turn to what is tab 4 in your binder, which is, as everyone will see, a rather large photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this large photograph is a printout from the audiovisual that you know as the Ljuboten panorama. Perhaps a copy of this could be placed on the ELMO for the public. It has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say, Mr. Saxon, that the last exhibit, the marking was lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we do that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hutsch is way ahead of both of us, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Could this particular image now be tendered into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be the exhibit just received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether perhaps the witness's copy of the -- of what is tab 4, if that could be moved onto the ELMO, please. Because we were not able to place this onto e-court in a way that we could annotate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, I need you to move that photograph on to this projector, so you can look at it there, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And perhaps if the audiovisual people could assist us by bringing the projector up as high as possible, so we can see as much of this image as possible. And then occasionally I may ask the witness to move the photograph from one side to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we talk about this image, Witness, going back to the policemen at this check-point, did they tell you why you couldn't pass through it?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: The police -- the policemen told us that there were ongoing police operation in the area of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is now on Friday, the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah, that's something -- something for -- of an operation was prepared something there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. If we take a look at this large photograph now, does this photograph describe the view that you had near that check-point on the afternoon of the 10th of August?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. It shows this view nearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And we see -- if you look at the bottom left-hand corner of the photograph, you see capital letters OP-1. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we agree that this photograph we will refer to it as observation point 1?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this photograph where you were standing you would be looking -- your view was from the south to the north, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now I need to ask you for your assistance a bit. Perhaps could you mark, in general, where, for example, the village of Ljubanci would be on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would ask if the counsel if he could move closer to the microphone, please, because we not able to hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that would be the eastern edge of the village of Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could help us, please, then perhaps to the left of that circle, could you write in not too large letters, the word "Ljubanci."

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving towards the right a little bit, a little bit further, please. No, to the right. Now, there we see now -- now near the centre of the photograph now, we see what appears to be the minaret of a mosque. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What village was that mosque in?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That's in the mosque of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So perhaps above the minaret, please, could you write the words "Ljuboten," the word "Ljuboten."

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could move the photograph back to the left, just a bit. All right. Now we see right now roughly in the centre of the photograph, in the foreground we see what appears to be a hill. You see this hill?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you were in that position on the 10th of August, 2001, how did you refer to this hill?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: This -- this hill --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: -- covers the western part of Ljuboten --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, no. You're not -- I'm sorry, my question was not clear. What did you call this hill?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: I was calling this hill out of a Serbian map, hill 631.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please write the numbers 631 on the side of that hill.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, you had been informed about this mine explosion, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that was in a place called Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this photograph can we see specifically the place called Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: We can just see it just roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, no, that is not my question. Can we see the place, the specific place called Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, could you please draw a circle approximately where it would be.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So it is somewhere up in a valley on the side of that ridge?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is on the other side of the ridge. That means you have to see behind this ridge and there it -- this place is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So to answer the question that I asked you before, that means if it is on the other side of this ridge from where you were standing you could not see it, could you?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you, above that circle, write the letters capital L and then capital B?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some point after the events in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, did you go personally to the spot known as Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. I did so when I was called up as a reserve officer to serve in the German embassy in Skopje. I went there in late October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, could this map please be marked for identification. I'll seek to tender it at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P292, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, when did you switch from working as a journalist to working as a reserve army officer?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: In the middle of September, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before that is removed, hold on, can we leave that there for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall while you were standing approximately around this spot, later in the afternoon what did you observe going on?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: I saw some single -- single rounds fired by mortars to the entrance and the outgoing of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To the entrance and to the exit of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But the entrance and the exit what directions are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Left side in my -- from my point of view, left side was the entrance --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would that be to the -- the western entrance?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. And then the exit would be on what side of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: On the eastern exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. You say you saw some mortar rounds. And where did these mortar rounds land?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: These mortar rounds land in the -- in the western entrance part of Ljuboten and in the eastern exit part of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. About how many rounds were fired, how many impacts did you see?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: All in all, between eight and ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, were you using binoculars to observe these events?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And what was your impression of this mortar fire, as a person with your military background?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: As a -- as a former forward observer, it was clear to me that the mortars started to fix target areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. All right. And why did you feel that way? Why did you form that opinion?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Because if this mortar fire should destroy or neutralise a position, you have to fire with a couple of mortars. That means with at least five, up to six mortars, because if you fire just one round, you can't with a mortar grenade hit exactly the point you would like to hit. The detonation is possibly between 50 and 100 metre away from the target. So just to have a result in the target, you have to -- to shoot with at least, yeah, five to six mortars or Howitzers into this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's in order to neutralise a target?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As opposed to fixing accuracy of --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- shooting? All right. At that time on this Friday afternoon, the 10th of August, did you observe any outgoing fire from the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No, I didn't observe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Had you been in places in Macedonia during the crisis time in 2001 where --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me finish my question. Had you been in places where Macedonian forces had fired on NLA positions?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in your experience, what was the response of the NLA?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: If you would say it a little bit kidding, you would say there was nothing coming in what wouldn't go out. So when a shot came in, the NLA immediately respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And, for example, where in Macedonia, what parts of Macedonia did you observe these kind of military dynamics?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: In the complete Tetovo area, Radusa area, Kumanovo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We mentioned Ljubotenski Bacila, and I don't want to forget that at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move to tab 5 of the binder, please, which is the photograph at page 6 of the court binder. It is 65 ter number 199.2, N004-4764.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, do you recognise the photograph that you see?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: It's the place where the ambush took place against the soldiers from the 2nd Company, 3rd battalion, 1st guard brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is this place known as Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it part of the populated region of the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just spend another moment, please, on what you saw on the Friday, 10th of August. If we could turn now to tab 6 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure if this -- excuse me. I'm not sure if the photograph of Ljubotenski Bacila is in evidence. If it is not, I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is not. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P293, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn to tab 6 of the binder, please, which is a panoramic photograph of Ljuboten that has been annotated. It's from 65 ter number 176. If that could be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hutsch, did you make the annotations on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does this photograph depict -- hmm, no. We need to go back to the colour photograph that we had before, if we can. Does this photograph depict now a view from north to south, going across the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And let's start, then, with the circle, there's a blue circle on the left-hand side, and there's a note underneath that, says "impacts 120-millimetre." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does that circle then describe?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That have been the two target areas that I saw on Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, I'm only referring to the circle on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That -- the left circle is one of the target areas I saw in the -- in the Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And by "the target areas," you mean of the mortar -- what appeared to you to be mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that left-hand circle, that would be the far eastern edge of the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Take a look at -- if we go towards the right now, we see an arrow, a thick arrow pointing down and then there's some -- there's half of a rectangle and some other markings and then the letters 120 and then the words "Nikola." What were you trying to depict there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: What I saw was that the fire that came to -- the target area was fired from the area of the monastery of Saint Nikola and in my point of view it had been fired by 120-millimetres mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just to go step by step. So this half of a rectangle above the number 120, that's -- that is not part of the photograph, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So that was your way of depicting approximately where this mortar position would have been, had the photograph been a bit bigger. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Why did you believe that the mortar fire -- let me go more slowly. The mortar fire that was being fired that day into the village of Ljuboten, do you know who was firing it?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: In this moment, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Why did you think it was 120-millimetre mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: The sound of a 120-millimetre mortar is -- is very deep, like an old man is angry and he shouts with somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. And that would be compared to what other kind of mortar, for example?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: For example, if you have an 82-metre mortar, it sounds more like a child is crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you use the sound of the fire to make a determination of the probable calibre of the mortar that was being fired?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You told me at that time on Friday afternoon, the 10th of August, you didn't know who was firing these shells. Did you subsequently find out who was doing this firing?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah. What we found out then in the evening with some phone calls is that the positions in the north of Ljuboten and Ljubanci were-- were in the end of the army and that these mortars are belonging to the army in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And if you go a bit further to the right, there's another blue circle, what appears to be the far western side of Ljuboten. What is depicted in that circle?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Here we have the other target area where single shells were fired in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told, Mr. Saxon, that this is one of seven photographs. Are you planning to use all seven?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not planning on using all seven. And if I can just clarify, I am planning on using a few other photographs in this range. But at this time, I would seek simply to tender this photograph with ERN number N001-7278.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is feasible and it will be done, but it means there has to be quite a process to extract one out of the seven. It will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will take that on board for the next time, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just it would be of assistance if we minimised that sort of inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If it would save work, then, Your Honour, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. It will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit P294, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a convenient time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. And we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly we'd like it apologise on behalf of our client. We have talked to the security. Our client was trying to get our attention to pass us a note and we have discussed with the security people who are sitting next to him and it is agreed that they would pass the paper on to us in the course of the proceedings. We have asked also our client not to pass this note too often so as not to disrupt the actual work and obligations of the security guards, but they've been very kind. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Now, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, I'd like to ask you, please, to turn your mind to the events of Saturday, 11th of August, 2001. Can you recall, please, what did you do on that Saturday morning, when you woke up?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: When I woke up we decided to go to Ljuboten area because we expected that something at that day would happen in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: "We" means in this moment the Macedonian interpreter and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when did you leave Skopje approximately?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Approximately a quarter to 7.00, 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you again drive towards the village of Radisani?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what were you driving in?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: We were driving all the time in a white Land Rover crusader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. And were there any special markings on this white Land Rover?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: We marked them as usual for war correspondents as a press car. That means we had a sign TV in front and on all the sides of this car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on this day, for example, were you and the interpreter wearing any special clothing?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No, we didn't wear special clothes but we had all the time in the car our flakjackets and helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you use the term "flakjacket," are you referring to something that is also known as a bullet-proof vest?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you arrive at the same check-point that we described earlier as observation point 1, that area?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: We found again the same police officers who are doing their duty there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was there any discussion between you and these police officers?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: There was a discussion if we could pass or if we couldn't pass, and I say in the -- in the normal way for the Balkans we solved this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, how you solved the problem?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: We gave over some bottles of beer, and in this case, 50 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who did you give the German marks to?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: To one of the, for me, active police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did you give the 50 German marks to this particular police officer?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: For me, it seems that he was in command of this check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And why did you conclude that this person was in command of the check-point? What led to you believe that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: He gave orders to the other police officers there. He, for example, sent one of the guys inside -- not inside, inside the car to -- to overview for me the radio communication or to control the other cars who were passing this check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. And you were then eventually allowed to pass through the check-point, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on that road then, were you proceeding towards Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, we were going to Ljubanci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you remember -- we're still talking about the morning of Saturday, 11 August, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately what time you arrived in Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And when you were in Ljubanci on that morning, were you able to observe positions of the army and the police in that village?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, please, to turn to what is tab 7 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There is 65 ter number 295. It has ERN number N001-7247. If that could be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, is this a map, the annotations on this map, did you produce them?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the designation that you have been putting -- that you have placed on this map and others like it that we've seen, did this come from the information you had written in your notebooks?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We'll discuss some of your notebooks later on. Perhaps let's just start with the -- the letters that are on the left side, please, we see the letters ARM and then MUP with an arrow pointed towards a village that I can see on my hard copy to be Ljubanci. Can you tell us what you were trying to depict there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That means that in the village of Ljubanci in this time there was a concentration and assembly area of -- of police forces and as well positions from soldiers that are belonging to the -- to the army of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to ask, please not to overlap, because it is impossible to interpret in this way. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have been instructed again that you and I need to pause a bit more between our sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could look directly to the right, on the -- further to the right, we see the number 2 and the number company and the number 2 and the word -- I'm sorry, number 2 and the word "company," and then the number 2 and the word "battalion." Is -- are both of those numbers correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is the mistake there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: It's the 2nd Company of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And is that referring to an army unit?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The army of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: The army of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, you need to pause between my question and your answer. Can you please take your marker, take the pen and draw a line through that incorrect number 2 and write the correct number that should be there next to it.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Down below, we see the number 3 Company and below that, 2 Battalion. Are both of those numbers correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No. Here we have also the 3rd Battalion, like I was writing in one sign and I was writing in this shot abbreviations as well, that it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: -- that these are units of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And by the 3rd Battalion, that is the 3rd battalion of the 1st Guardist Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Of the Macedonian army?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you draw a line that you that inaccurate number 2, please, and write the letter 3 again.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. If you can move now more towards the centre of the map, we see an arrow pointing towards the north-east and we see the word "mortars." And underneath that arrow there's a line. Can you explain what you were trying to depict there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: With this marking with this position, I tried to -- to make clear that there have been the mortar position from the army in the area of the monastery Saint Nikola.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, for the record, the witness has drawn a red line above the numbers 2.1. And if you could, please -- there's below the number 2.1, we see a line that appears to go, I hope I'm saying this accurately, from the north-west towards the south-east. What does that blue line show?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: This blue line shows the positions of the 2nd Company of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Of the Macedonian army?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So is it correct then to interpret your annotations as that the 2nd Company of the 3rd Battalion was somewhere in an elevation above the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly. They have been north and north-east of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P295, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, could you please turn to what is tab 8 of your binder. And this is again -- this is again from 65 ter number 295. The ERN of this map is N001-7248. Mr. Hutsch, did you produce this sketch?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier -- I'll step back for a moment. In general terms, what does this sketch represent, just in general terms?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: It shows the village of Ljubanci, and inside this village some assembly areas from the police forces and a headquarter of the army as well as a logistical centre from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to take this now more step by step. And does this sketch depict what you saw then on the morning of Saturday, 11 August?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. We see in the middle -- first of all, it looks like you've drawn a little -- my mind is not working as quickly as it should. You're indicating that word -- the MUP on the lower left-hand side means assembly areas of MUP and in this case by "MUP," you're referring to the Macedonian police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the letters VVD, what do those letters refer to?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That means a forward logistical centre of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that battalion would have been of the Macedonian army?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe -- for example, let's just stick with the police units that you saw in these assembly areas. Can you-- first of all, how did you know that these were police?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: You could see camouflaged and uniforms in majority and minority black overalls, and all these uniforms were marked with this police badge we saw before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see any -- and if we can -- if I can just ask you, because you mentioned army, and you mentioned police. On that day where did you see -- where did you primarily see members of the army?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Members of the army I saw primarily in the area of the school where I was told that the headquarter of the 3rd Battalion was located, and I saw them close to the monastery of Saint Nikola, in a house and by -- both sites of the street close to that monastery where they located their logistical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see members of the army above Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. I saw single positions from the -- the army in the north and north-east of the Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how far above Ljuboten in those hills would you estimate those army positions were?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: A direction I suppose between 700 metre and 1.5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned, first of all, that the -- the army of Macedonia had a command post or a headquarters at the school. In the centre of this sketch, we see a blue circle around a rectangle that's marked "school." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how did you know, for example, that they were -- the persons headquartered there were members of the army?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: This school was guarded by army soldiers, and inside the schoolyard you could see vehicles of the army with the number plates as well of the army, and there were some blue Hummer commanding vehicles, and these light brown army vehicles that you saw usually with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you were able to distinguish between uniforms worn by army soldiers and uniforms worn by police officers?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly what the difference was? What did the army uniforms look like at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: The army uniforms in this time have been light brown with -- with dark brown, black points inside, and the -- the police uniforms, they were looking very similar to the -- the American uniforms. That means they were more camouflaged in green/brown colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And, of course, the insignia or patches would have been different?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. Because the army, they were having the flag of Macedonia, the Republic of Macedonia on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could estimate -- actually, you also mention a logistics centre. And where was that? The logistics centre of the army. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That was on the road from Ljubanci to the monastery of Saint Nikola. I think the commanding post of this logistical centre was in the building close to the monastery if you are going north right side the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know in normal times what that building was used for?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: I was told that it was planned to -- to -- to establish their-- something like a hotel for pilgrims who would go to the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see a building there known as the children's rest home?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: The term children's rest house, I learned later on when I was a reserve officer in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And do you now associate this logistics centre in any way with the children rest home?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah. It was the commanding post and some of the logistical things were inside this rest house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If you could estimate -- well, let me start again. Did you see any -- first of all, did you see any armoured vehicles in Ljubanci that morning?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, in the entrance, if you -- in the south entrance of Ljubanci, you could see two BTR APCs hardly south the football field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know to which institution these APCs belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: They belonged to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: There were police badges like the normal police officers were wearing on their uniforms on these APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And you described these APCs or armoured personnel carriers as BTR. Would this be the same kind of APC as what was known as a Hermelin or is a Hermelin a different kind of APC?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: A Hermelin is a -- a Hermelin is a different kind of APC. It's more light than the BTR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And did you see any weapons mounted on these APCs on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: They were the normal equipment or the normal arm. That means they had 14.5-millimetre machine-gun in top of the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Going back now to what is circled as the school on your sketch here, you mentioned that it was some kind of command post or a headquarters. Do you know if there were any police commanders present at this school on that day?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: In the schoolyard, I could see a mixture between these commanding vehicles of the army as well as normal police vehicles like Cherokee jeeps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But my question was: "Do you know if there were -- did you form any opinion as to whether there were any police commanders present?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: What I saw as well was that some police commanders, officers entered the school. By the behaviour of these police officers, I suppose that they are commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And why did you draw or form that opinion? What was it about the behaviour of these gentlemen or the persons around them that made you form that opinion?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: First they were saluted by the guards. Second, they gave orders to their drivers to drive away the car from the entrance to a parking place, and they came out and shouted to some drivers and then these drivers drove away to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Was there anything in particular that you noticed about these Jeep Cherokees from the police?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were some Jeep Cherokees, Cherokee Jeeps?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From the police. Was there anything about the equipment on these jeeps that drew your attention?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: These Cherokee jeeps were equipped with -- with radio communication, and you could see with this radio communication that they are -- and also in my experience to that point, that they are used as commanding vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How many antennas did these jeeps have?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: These jeep had one antenna and one radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did that indicate you that these jeeps belonged to commanders or were command vehicles?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: For example, you have had other jeeps, mostly Lada jeeps who didn't have any radio communication and they just had mobile radio communication to use it for commanding or for patrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So what was special about the radio equipment on these --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: They had a --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- jeeps that you saw?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: -- fix -- they had a fixed radio communication set inside the jeep and that means also one antenna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And why did that indicate to you that the person moving around in that jeep would be a commander?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Because what I saw is that in the past, what I saw in the past, that these Cherokee jeeps were given to commanders as a commanding vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Because they needed special communication equipment.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah, they need special communication equipment to cover their patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Tell us a bit, please, about -- first of all, you describe here on this sketch several different assembly points of police officers. I can see four, four circles. Approximately how many police officers did you see assembled in Ljubanci there on that day? Actually -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Between 100 and 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you observe about these police officers? How were they behaving?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: These officers were preparing shall -- were preparing something, an operation because, for example, they were putting ammunition into their magazines. They were preparing their personal equipment, like they were -- yeah, looking for their bullet-proof vests. They were looking for their helmets. They were preparing rucksacks with water and some food. And it was all close together. That means not one of these soldiers or these police officers was far away from his personal equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did the filling of magazines with ammunition, filling of rucksacks, et cetera, why did that indicate to you that these police officers were preparing for an operation?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: So they -- they have been armed. They have been provided with ammunition. You won't do that without just -- just for -- for holiday trip or for an exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. And the filling of rucksacks. What did that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: That prepares -- that shows me that, yeah, they would leave Ljubanci because in Ljubanci they could get water everywhere in every house. Just if they would like to leave Ljubanci into another place, they would use water in bottles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Did you have any conversations with any of these police officers?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yeah. We had conversation to some of these police officers, but nothing what was going into -- into depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But even without going into depth can you recall more or less what some of these police officers said?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: They said, yeah, we have to fight against the terrorists. We have to -- to fight against terrorists in Ljuboten. We are going to fight them, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Did they make any references to the mine explosion at Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: There was I thought, like, angriness among them, because some of their comrades died there or some of the Macedonian security forces died there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you observe amongst these policemens, a group 100 or 150, did you observe any lack of discipline?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No, there were no a lack of discipline. They were highly disciplined, these soldiers. I didn't see one bottle of beer among them. There were nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Earlier you mentioned that some of these police officers were wearing black overalls with police patches. Do you remember telling me that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I want to explore this with you a little bit, please. Prior to the events in Ljuboten, were there any, you know, perhaps mid-July, sometime in July, were there any rumours going around or information circulating among the journalists about new units in the Macedonian police?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes. It was the rumour that in the Ministry of Interior some new units have been built up, have been founded. And these units would have been under the direct command of the Minister of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what information did you have as to the minister's -- well, what information did you have as to the reason for the establishment of these units? What led to the establishment of them?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: So I did an interview with the minister of defence in the beginning of August, and he disagreed with the -- with the way the Minister of the Interior would like to handle the crisis. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One second. If we can just go a bit more slowly. That Defence Minister was Mr. -- at the time, 2001, that was Vlado Buckovski, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you describe a little bit more precisely what the nature -- what was the nature of the disagreement that Minister Buckovski described between himself and Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: The defence minister would like or saw the future of Macedonia in -- in a cooperation -- not a cooperation, in a common life between all the ethnical groups. That means for him, he would like to deal and to manage the crisis, but he's -- his focus was on the future. And the Minister of Interior tried to fight against the NLA in the most hardest way and purpose to destroy them, and he doesn't have a -- an option or a -- a vision about the future for the former -- for the future Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how did you relate this information -- well let me step back for a minute. During this interview with the defence minister what if anything did the defence minister tell you about future joint operations between the army and police?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: He said that there will be -- that in his point of view there shouldn't be any more combined joint operations between the army and the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That was because he and Mr. Boskoski did not agree?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As to how to conduct the war?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if we can move back to this information that you had received about the formation of new police units in the Ministry of the Interior, so what, then, did you understand -- what was the information that you received for -- in terms of the purpose of these new units or unit?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: So, it became more and more clear in the time, I will say, until October and November, so these units were equipped, that they could -- could fight on their own without support from the army, and they were also trained to fight alone without support of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was your understanding -- to whom -- who would benefit from the establishment of these units?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: The Minister of Interior himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Because he had a couple of special units who would follow his personal order and in my personal point of view, he did something -- he created something like his pretorians [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I want to go back now to this issue of the black overalls. You saw some police officers in Ljubanci that Saturday wearing black overalls?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With police insignia. On that Saturday, did you make any connection between police officers wearing black overalls and the information you had received about creation of new Special Units?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P296, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you remember until -- approximately how much time did you spend in Ljubanci on that Saturday?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Between four and five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you observe any -- well, let me start again. Did you hear or observe any shooting, any kind of shooting that Saturday?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: What I heard is some machine-gun fire from the positions of the 2nd Company towards Ljuboten, and I heard again some single rounds that were fired by mortars into Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you ascertain or judge who was firing the single rounds into Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: They came from the mortars in the area of the monastery of Saint Nikola.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that indicated to you what, that they were coming from which force?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: From the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Again, what opinion did you draw, or conclusion, from your observations of these single rounds being directed into Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: They didn't make a right sense to me in the first, but if you think about that, it was also some rounds that were fired to fix the target areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So it was a similar situation to what you had observed on Friday, the 10th?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. Would this a convenient time to stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if I could simply just clarify an issue of witness scheduling, Your Honour, this witness cannot arrive back in The Hague in time for court on Monday. Therefore, on Monday, we will continue with the next witness on our schedule, finish that witness, hopefully on Monday or Tuesday, and then Mr. Hutsch will be back to finish his evidence during the remainder of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have we caught up with all the witnesses who fell by the wayside?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There is one witness who was ill last week, and we knew that -- well, let me start again. Because there were several witnesses last week who were ill, two of which began their testimony, we knew because of certain commitments to witness scheduling this week and next that we couldn't bring -- we couldn't keep both of the ill witnesses here, so there is one witness who the Prosecution will bring back hopefully in about two weeks' time to finish his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We must now adjourn, and we resume on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
